triage.name: Periorbital cellulitis
triage.reason: Eyelid and preseptal swelling after local trauma or sinusitis; diagnosis by history and exam, with orbital cellulitis as the critical look-alike.

demographics: Most common in young children; about two-thirds of cases occur in children under 10 years
Adults account for a minority of cases and often have a preceding sinus infection or local skin injury

risk_factors.text: Recent upper respiratory infection or sinusitis
Local eyelid or periorbital skin injury, insect bite, or animal bite
Recent eye surgery or periorbital procedure

exposures: Animal bites or scratches near the eye
Contact with someone who has conjunctivitis

chief_complaints.text: My eye is swollen and red
My eyelid is puffy and warm

hpi.onset: Gradual over hours to a day or two, often after a cold, sinus infection, or a small injury or bug bite near the eye
hpi.progression: Swelling and redness build up over the first day or two; the eye itself stays comfortable to look through and vision does not change
hpi.location: Around one eye, involving the eyelid and skin in front of the orbital septum
hpi.quality: Tender, warm, puffy swelling of the eyelid and surrounding skin
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; uncomfortable but not severe

associated_symptoms.text: Redness of the skin around the eye
Runny or stuffy nose from a recent cold

argues_against: Severe sinus tenderness with high fever

positives.text: Warmth and redness of the skin around the eye

atypical.how_it_differs: Young children may only be fussy, rub the eye, or refuse to open it; fever and eyelid swelling can be the only findings.
missing_classic_features: Localizing history of trauma or sinus symptoms

atypical.how_it_differs: May have less fever and less pain than expected, and swelling can be mistaken for allergic or age-related eyelid changes.
Can progress faster and with fewer classic signs; a mild-looking eyelid swelling may mask a deeper infection.

general.mild: Well-appearing, comfortable, no distress; eyelid swelling and redness only
general.moderate: Mildly uncomfortable, low-grade fever, eyelid swollen shut or nearly shut
general.severe: Ill-appearing, febrile, marked periorbital swelling with pain
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, lethargic, or signs of orbital or intracranial extension (proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, vision loss, meningismus)

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin around the eye
findings.finding: Redness and warmth of the periorbital skin

findings.maneuver: Palpate the swollen eyelid and periorbital skin gently
findings.finding: Tenderness of the eyelid and periorbital tissues

findings.maneuver: Inspect the eyes from above and below for forward displacement of the globe
Test extraocular movements in all directions
findings.finding: No ophthalmoplegia; full, painless eye movements

findings.maneuver: Check visual acuity and confrontational visual fields
findings.finding: No decrease in visual acuity or visual field loss

findings.maneuver: Ask about or observe pain during eye movements
Check for neck stiffness and perform Kernig and Brudzinski signs if meningitis is suspected
Palpate or percuss the frontal and maxillary sinuses

Limited evaluation of the orbital apex and sinuses

imaging.study: Plain radiograph of the orbits or sinuses

initial.why: Leukocytosis with a left shift supports a bacterial infection and helps gauge severity
Baseline electrolytes and renal function before antibiotics
Rules out pregnancy before CT imaging

initial.test: CT orbits and sinuses with IV contrast
initial.why: Distinguishes preseptal from orbital cellulitis and identifies sinusitis or abscess
initial.only_if: proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, vision change, severe pain, or failure to improve on antibiotics

supporting.why: Adds evidence of inflammation but does not localize the infection
May identify a pathogen in febrile or systemically ill patients
supporting.only_if: fever, toxic appearance, or suspected bacteremia

supporting.test: MRI orbits with and without IV contrast
supporting.why: Avoids radiation and better evaluates intracranial extension
supporting.only_if: pregnancy or suspected intracranial or cavernous sinus involvement

not_indicated.test: Plain radiograph of the orbits or sinuses
not_indicated.why: Does not distinguish preseptal from orbital cellulitis and rarely changes management
Limited evaluation of the orbit and sinuses; CT is preferred when orbital involvement is suspected
Not needed unless intracranial extension or meningeal signs are suspected
not_indicated.only_if: meningeal signs, altered mental status, or suspected intracranial extension

not_indicated.why: Not routinely needed unless sepsis is suspected
Not routinely needed for uncomplicated preseptal cellulitis
not_indicated.only_if: systemic infection or sepsis is suspected

not_indicated.why: No role unless meningitis is suspected
not_indicated.only_if: meningeal signs or altered mental status

decision_points: Pregnancy test before CT in anyone who could be pregnant
Check visual acuity, extraocular movements, and proptosis before deciding on imaging
Proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, vision loss, or severe pain should prompt urgent CT and ophthalmology involvement
Children who are well-appearing with isolated preseptal findings may be managed without imaging

differential.name: Orbital cellulitis
differential.why_considered: Same periorbital swelling and redness, but infection has crossed the orbital septum into the orbit; this is the critical look-alike because it threatens vision and can spread intracranially.
differential.trigger: Proptosis, painful or limited eye movements, decreased visual acuity, or a swollen eye that is not improving on oral antibiotics

exam: Ophthalmoplegia or pain on extraocular movements
Decreased visual acuity or abnormal pupillary response
imaging: CT orbits with contrast showing orbital fat stranding, extraocular muscle enlargement, or subperiosteal abscess
Opacification of adjacent ethmoid or maxillary sinuses
MRI showing orbital or intracranial extension when suspected

differential.name: Allergic contact dermatitis of the eyelid
differential.why_considered: Eyelid swelling and redness can look like preseptal cellulitis, especially after a new cosmetic, soap, or eye drop.

history: Exposure to a new cosmetic, soap, sunscreen, or eye drop
No fever or preceding sinus infection
exam: Eczematous, scaly, or vesicular eyelid skin
Conjunctiva may be mildly injected but not purulent
labs: Normal white count and inflammatory markers
imaging: Not indicated; no orbital or sinus abnormality

differential.name: Angioedema
differential.why_considered: Rapid, painless eyelid and periorbital swelling can mimic cellulitis, particularly when it is asymmetric or follows a trigger.
differential.trigger: Rapid onset of painless, non-tender swelling, especially with lip, tongue, or airway involvement

history: Sudden onset over minutes to hours
New medication (ACE inhibitor), food, or insect exposure
History of similar episodes or urticaria
exam: Possible lip, tongue, or airway swelling
labs: Normal white count and inflammatory markers
C4 and C1 inhibitor levels if hereditary angioedema is suspected
imaging: Not routinely needed; CT orbits normal if obtained

differential.name: Conjunctivitis
differential.why_considered: Red, watery eye with eyelid swelling can be mistaken for early preseptal cellulitis, especially in children.

history: Itching or burning rather than deep pain
Recent upper respiratory infection or sick contacts
No fever or periorbital skin erythema
exam: Eyelid swelling is mild and limited to the lid margin
No periorbital skin erythema or tenderness

differential.name: Dacryocystitis
differential.why_considered: Infection of the lacrimal sac causes medial canthal swelling and redness that can spread to the periorbital tissues.

history: Pain and swelling localized to the medial canthus
Recurrent episodes or known nasolacrimal duct obstruction
exam: Tender, erythematous swelling over the lacrimal sac
Expression of pus from the punctum
imaging: CT may show lacrimal sac enlargement and adjacent inflammation

differential.name: Cavernous sinus thrombosis
differential.why_considered: A rare but life-threatening complication of periorbital or sinus infection that can present with eyelid swelling and redness.
differential.trigger: Bilateral eye findings, severe headache, cranial nerve palsies, or rapid progression despite antibiotics

exam: Cranial nerve III, IV, V1, V2, or VI deficits
imaging: MRI with MR venography showing filling defect in the cavernous sinus
CT with contrast may show enlargement and enhancement of the cavernous sinus

differential.name: Orbital tumor
differential.why_considered: A mass lesion in the orbit can cause proptosis and eyelid swelling, though it is usually more gradual and non-infectious.
differential.trigger: Gradual, painless proptosis or persistent swelling without fever or signs of infection

history: Gradual onset over weeks to months
Possible visual changes or double vision
exam: Possible optic disc swelling or atrophy
imaging: CT or MRI showing a discrete orbital mass

severity.mild: Early, uncomplicated: eyelid swelling and redness only, no fever or low-grade fever, well-appearing, no orbital signs
severity.moderate: Established: swollen eyelid nearly shut, fever, mild leukocytosis, but no proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, or vision change
severity.severe: Marked periorbital swelling with pain, high fever, significant leukocytosis, or failure to improve on oral antibiotics; concern for orbital extension
severity.critical: Orbital or intracranial extension with proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, vision loss, meningismus, altered mental status, or sepsis

red_flags.meaning: Suggests orbital cellulitis or an orbital mass; needs urgent imaging and ophthalmology involvement

red_flags.finding: Pain with eye movement or ophthalmoplegia
red_flags.meaning: Indicates orbital involvement; risk of vision loss

red_flags.finding: Decreased visual acuity or abnormal pupillary response
red_flags.meaning: Optic nerve or orbital apex involvement; emergency

red_flags.finding: Bilateral eye findings or cranial nerve palsies
Meningismus, severe headache, or altered mental status

red_flags.meaning: Sepsis; needs resuscitation and IV antibiotics

red_flags.finding: Failure to improve after 24–48 hours of appropriate oral antibiotics
red_flags.meaning: Consider orbital cellulitis, abscess, or resistant organism

complications.name: Subperiosteal abscess
clues: CT showing medial orbital wall abscess

special_populations.differences: Most common in children under 10; may present with fussiness, eye rubbing, or refusal to open the eye rather than clear pain. Fever and eyelid swelling may be the only findings. Orbital cellulitis can progress quickly, so a low threshold for imaging and admission is warranted.
May have less fever and less pain than expected; swelling can be mistaken for allergic or age-related eyelid changes. Higher risk of atypical presentation and delayed diagnosis.
Can progress faster with fewer classic signs; a mild-looking eyelid swelling may mask a deeper infection. Consider broader empiric antibiotics and a lower threshold for imaging and admission.
Avoid CT if possible; MRI without contrast is preferred when imaging is needed. Antibiotic choices should be reviewed for pregnancy safety.

key_questions.question: When did the swelling start, and how quickly has it changed?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over hours to 1–2 days; rapid progression over hours suggests orbital cellulitis or angioedema

key_questions.question: Did this start after a cold, sinus infection, or an injury or bug bite near the eye?
key_questions.looking_for: Preceding upper respiratory infection, sinusitis, or local skin trauma or insect bite

key_questions.question: Is there any bulging of the eye, double vision, or pain when you move the eye?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; any of these suggests orbital cellulitis rather than preseptal infection

key_questions.question: Has your vision changed at all — blurring, loss of vision, or trouble seeing out of the corner of your eye?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; decreased visual acuity or visual field loss points to orbital or optic nerve involvement

key_questions.question: Have you had a fever, chills, or felt generally unwell?
key_questions.looking_for: Low-grade fever and mild malaise are common; high fever or toxic appearance raises concern for deeper infection

key_questions.question: Does the eye itself hurt, itch, or have discharge?
key_questions.looking_for: Itching without pain suggests allergic contact dermatitis; purulent discharge suggests conjunctivitis or dacryocystitis

key_questions.question: Have you had a severe headache, neck stiffness, confusion, or any seizure?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; these suggest meningitis, cavernous sinus thrombosis, or intracranial extension

key_questions.question: Have you had any recent eye surgery or a procedure around the eye?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent surgery increases risk and may warrant broader antibiotic coverage and imaging

key_questions.question: Do you have any condition or take any medicine that weakens your immune system?
key_questions.looking_for: Immunosuppressive therapy such as prednisone, or an immunocompromising condition; lowers the threshold for imaging and admission

key_questions.question: Have you started any new cosmetic, soap, sunscreen, or eye drop, or had a similar episode before?
key_questions.looking_for: New topical exposure or recurrent itching episodes suggests allergic contact dermatitis

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Determines need for pregnancy testing before CT imaging and guides antibiotic choice

key_questions.question: Any allergies to antibiotics, especially penicillins or cephalosporins?

reasoning_points: Eyelid and periorbital swelling with redness and warmth, often after a cold, sinus infection, or local skin injury or insect bite
Low-grade fever and mild leukocytosis may be present but are not required
The critical distinction is preseptal versus orbital cellulitis: absence of proptosis, pain with eye movement, ophthalmoplegia, and vision change supports a preseptal process
Visual acuity, extraocular movements, and inspection for proptosis are checked before deciding on imaging
CT orbits and sinuses with contrast is reserved for suspected orbital extension, proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, vision change, severe pain, or failure to improve on antibiotics
Pregnancy must be excluded before CT in anyone who could be pregnant
Look-alikes such as allergic contact dermatitis, angioedema, conjunctivitis, dacryocystitis, orbital cellulitis, and cavernous sinus thrombosis are considered and excluded by history and exam

easy: Young child with a recent cold or bug bite near the eye
Unilateral swollen, red, tender eyelid with low-grade fever
No proptosis, full painless eye movements, and normal vision
Mild leukocytosis and no orbital signs
medium: Adult with preceding sinusitis and periorbital swelling but no orbital signs
Eyelid swollen shut with fever and leukocytosis, requiring a careful orbital exam
Itching and a new cosmetic exposure suggesting allergic contact dermatitis rather than infection
Medial canthal swelling and tearing suggesting dacryocystitis
hard: Young child who is fussy and refuses to open the eye, with fever as the only finding
Older adult with minimal fever and swelling mistaken for allergic or age-related eyelid changes
Immunocompromised patient with mild-looking swelling that masks deeper infection
Rapidly progressive bilateral eye findings with headache or cranial nerve palsies suggesting cavernous sinus thrombosis
Failure to improve after 24–48 hours of appropriate oral antibiotics, raising concern for orbital cellulitis or abscess
